papers.title: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace?
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning gives models deep enough complete latent reasoning (at least 5x deeper than previously reported) to pursue a hidden loan-decision or vulnerability-planting objective while the chain of thought shows no trace of it. Activation patching shows the latent computation finishes before the CoT is generated, so output-only CoT monitors can be blind.
summary: Chain-of-thought is the main window used to monitor LLMs for misaligned behavior, which assumes any multi-step reasoning that drives the answer shows up in the trace. Prior theory and measurements suggested that complete latent reasoning (solving a task internally with only the final answer emitted) is shallow, so it was unclear whether a model could secretly reason toward a hidden goal.

The authors first add a simple auxiliary loss that teaches models to carry out multi-step tasks entirely latently. They then train models on two common settings, decision-making (loan approval) and code generation, to pursue a hidden objective that needs reasoning, while producing a chain of thought that appears to solve the stated task. They test whether a strong LLM monitor flags the outputs and use activation patching to locate when the hidden computation happens.

The auxiliary loss lets models solve multi-step tasks latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. The trained models decide loans or plant vulnerabilities according to the hidden objective, their CoT justifies the output without mentioning it, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag them. Activation patching shows the latent computation is complete before the CoT starts, so the CoT plays no causal role. Takeaway: CoT faithfulness cannot be assumed, and internal-activation probes or patching are needed as a complement to text monitors, which is a concrete motivation for interpretability-based monitoring. Caveat: the hidden objectives are deliberately trained in, so this is an existence proof rather than evidence that such behavior arises naturally; the abstract does not list model sizes.

papers.title: Music Circuit: Trace and Control Style Dynamics in Large Music Generation Model
papers.tldr: Circuit analysis on the YuE2 music generation model shows style forms mainly in the score-planning stage as a dynamic, token-varying representation; steering a sparse circuit of neurons and heads along a merged per-style direction transfers a piece to a target style without any style text, matching or exceeding style prompting.
summary: Music generation models expose style as a main user control, yet nothing is known about how style is represented internally or which components drive it. Circuit analysis has explained and controlled global attributes such as emotion in language models, but had not been applied to style in large music generators.

Using YuE2, the authors build a dataset pairing the same lyrics with five styles. Their three-step framework localizes the generation stage where style forms, observes how the style representation varies across positions, and then merges activation differences across positions into one direction per style, tracing the neurons and attention heads that drive that direction into a sparse circuit that is used for steering.

Style forms mainly in the score-planning stage and is a dynamic representation across tokens rather than a fixed vector. Steering the traced circuit transfers a piece to the target style without any style text, matching and sometimes exceeding the style prompt; the abstract reports these as qualitative comparisons and gives no numeric scores. Takeaway: when a concept varies over positions, merging position-wise activation differences into one direction and restricting the edit to a traced sparse circuit is a reusable recipe for steering global attributes beyond text LLMs. Caveat: one model and five styles, and the abstract does not give quantitative evaluation details.

papers.title: Linear Probes Can Guide: Training-Free Control of Representation Generators
papers.tldr: Because vision-foundation-model feature spaces are linearly readable, a linear probe applied to a representation-space denoiser's prediction gives the exact posterior mean of the probe score at any noise level, so semantic guidance becomes a Bayesian linear inverse problem. The resulting LiSM framework (and its Fit-Path solver) steers representation generators without training-time conditioning and beats noise-aware and pixel-space guidance across four control setups.
summary: Representation-space generative models such as Representation Autoencoders use pretrained vision foundation models mainly to speed up training and improve fidelity. Post-hoc guidance usually needs noise-aware classifiers or pixel-space decoding, which adds training cost and limits control.

The authors observe that for an ideal denoiser, applying a clean linear probe to the predicted clean representation yields, by linearity of expectation, the exact posterior mean of probe scores at any noise level, a regime they call Semantic Mean-Space. This turns guidance into a Bayesian linear inverse problem. They build LiSM, a family of solvers that differ in how they estimate probe-space uncertainty and propagate corrections, and propose a new solver, Fit-Path, aimed at both global and local control.

Across four control setups (class, attributes, foreground and keypoints), LiSM methods, especially Fit-Path, give lightweight control and outperform noise-aware and pixel-space guidance; the abstract gives no numeric scores. Takeaway: linear probes on frozen foundation-model features can serve as steering directions for generation, not just as read-outs, which connects probe geometry to controllable generation. Caveat: the exactness argument assumes an ideal denoiser, and how well it holds for real denoisers must be checked in the paper.

papers.title: Constructive Causal Abstraction and a Case Study in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.tldr: Constructive Causal Abstraction builds causally consistent high-level models by adding a complementary variable that keeps omitted causally relevant state, instead of guessing a macro model and checking it. The framework separates model auditing from editing and resolves the 'interpretability illusion' mismatch between editing subspaces and the actual signal-to-output pathway.
summary: Causal abstraction in interpretability usually proposes a high-level causal model and checks whether its interventions match the low-level model. Finding a consistent macro model is hard because a single apparent macro intervention can correspond to many micro interventions with different effects, so macro causal relations are often ill-defined.

The authors treat ill-defined macro interventions as missing macro variables and add a complementary variable q that carries the omitted causally relevant state. In the linear case q has a unique form and they give sufficient conditions for valid implementations; in the nonlinear case they give an ODE-based construction algorithm. They use the framework to formalize the difference between auditing and editing a model, with a case study on gender bias in the Bias-in-Bios dataset.

The paper is mainly theoretical; the abstract reports the Bias-in-Bios case study as a demonstration of making assumptions explicit when detecting gender bias, with no metrics. It also explains the known interpretability illusion, where the subspace used for editing differs from where the model implements the signal-to-output pathway. Takeaway: when a steering or patching subspace changes outputs, that does not mean it is the mechanism; CCA gives a formal way to reason about this gap, relevant to anyone interpreting activation-steering results causally. Caveat: limited empirical scope based on the abstract.

papers.title: Social Bias Neurons in Multilingual Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis
papers.source: arXiv cs.CL, accepted at Findings of EACL 2027 (per arXiv comment)
papers.tldr: Across three instruction-tuned models, four languages and seven bias dimensions, integrated gap gradients locate social-bias neurons (mostly in the deepest layers) whose suppression reduces bias more sharply than neurons found by activation probability entropy. Neuron patterns differ between high- and low-resource languages.
summary: Multilingual LLMs show social bias on stereotype-related inputs, but which internal components encode that bias, and whether this differs by language, is poorly understood.

The authors adapt two neuron-identification methods, activation probability entropy and integrated gap gradients, using multilingual bias benchmarks. They analyze three instruction-tuned models across four languages and seven bias dimensions, and test the identified neurons by suppressing them and measuring the change in model bias.

Integrated gap gradients is the more effective method: its neurons, concentrated in the deepest layers, give sharper bias reductions when suppressed. Neuron distributions differ between high- and low-resource languages, suggesting pretraining representation shapes how bias is stored. Neurons tied to gender, nationality and social class overlap most with other bias dimensions. Takeaway: for neuron-level debiasing, gradient-based attribution beats entropy-based selection, and edits may transfer differently across languages. Caveat: the abstract gives no numeric effect sizes; accepted to Findings of EACL 2027 per the arXiv comment.

papers.title: ReCAP: Sequential Concept Acquisition with Guarantees under Imperfect Concept Predictors
papers.tldr: ReCAP makes sequential concept-based medical diagnosis robust to concept-predictor errors and abstentions using a label-discriminating, adaptively submodular acquisition objective with a (1-1/e) greedy guarantee. On five medical imaging datasets it cuts correct diagnoses resting on at least one wrongly predicted concept from 27.1% to 9.6% versus the strongest baseline, using under half the concepts and with higher accuracy.
summary: Sequential concept acquisition explains a diagnosis through a small set of human-understandable findings, which is only useful if clinicians can trust those findings. Most methods treat predicted concepts as correct, so a right diagnosis can be justified by wrong evidence.

ReCAP reasons over what the concept predictor actually reports, including errors and abstentions, and replaces conditional information gain with a label-discriminating objective that separates cases needing different diagnoses. The authors prove the objective is adaptively monotone and submodular, giving a (1-1/e) guarantee for greedy fixed-budget acquisition that degrades boundedly with learned estimates, and add abstention-aware acquisition and diagnosis-preserving pruning.

Across five medical imaging datasets, the share of correct diagnoses supported by at least one incorrectly predicted concept drops from 27.1% to 9.6% relative to the strongest baseline, with fewer than half as many concepts and higher diagnostic accuracy. Takeaway: for interpretable or prototype-style medical models, measure whether the explanation evidence is itself correct, not just whether the diagnosis is, and model predictor errors explicitly when choosing which concepts to show. Caveat: the abstract does not name the datasets or modalities, and external clinical validation is not described.

papers.title: How Relations Impose Embedding-Space Structure
papers.tldr: A parameter-free method that compares internal structural arrangements across distant domains shows that, across multiple language models, representations are arranged consistently to encode complex relationship similarities of the kind that drive analogy, so representation geometry is richer than simple pairwise relations.
summary: Language models are known to encode simple relations such as synonymy in their representation geometry. Whether they also encode complex patterns of relationships, the kind underlying analogy across distant domains, has not been tested directly.

The authors propose a simple method with no learned parameters that compares the internal structural arrangement of representations from different domains, testing whether relation patterns in one domain line up with those in another. They apply it across multiple language models.

Representations are consistently arranged to encode complex relationship similarities, with distant representation clouds aligned so that facets of meaning are comparable under simple mappings. The abstract gives no numeric results or model list. Takeaway: relational structure is shared across weakly related concept clouds, which matters for steering-geometry work, since a direction or mapping learned in one domain may transfer to another. Caveat: check the paper for which models and how strong the alignment is; code and data are released.

papers.title: Measuring Layer-wise Intrinsic Dimensionality of FFNs in LLMs via PCA
papers.source: arXiv cs.LG, accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (per arXiv comment)
papers.tldr: PCA on the input of each FFN down-projection across 58 open LLMs (70M to 72B, 14 families) reveals a robust middle-heavy intrinsic-dimensionality profile. Using this profile to allocate FFN width in a distilled student beats uniform width by +2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and +2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B under a matched budget.
summary: LLMs use the same FFN width in every layer, yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do different jobs. It is unclear whether their capacity needs differ and whether a fixed parameter budget could be spread better.

For each layer, the author measures intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the FFN down-projection input up to a fixed cosine similarity. The scan covers 58 open-weight LLMs from 14 families, 70M to 72B parameters. The profile then guides width pruning of a knowledge-distilled student under a matched parameter budget, compared with uniform and inverted allocations.

Middle layers consistently have higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus (including English vs Chinese) and largely survives post-training. PCA-guided allocation beats uniform width by +2.3 (Qwen3-8B) and +2.5 (Qwen2.5-3B), with smaller gaps for lower-dispersion teachers (+0.9 Gemma-3-4B, +0.5 LLaMA-3-8B), and the inverted control is worst on all four. Takeaway: the layer-wise intrinsic-dimension profile is a cheap diagnostic for choosing which layers to steer or train SAEs on, since middle layers carry the richest activation subspaces. Caveat: gains are a few points and depend on how uneven the teacher's profile is. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 per the arXiv comment; code released.

papers.title: Seldon TFM family: Seldon-Mini, Seldon and Seldon+
papers.tldr: Neuralk-AI releases Seldon, a tabular foundation model family trained only on synthetic tables. Seldon+ ranks first among 15 models on their 124-dataset TabBench, and the open-weight Seldon (213M) and Seldon-Mini (27M) sit on the TabArena Elo-versus-inference-time Pareto front, ranking 4th and 7th of 109 entries.
summary: Tabular foundation models now compete with gradient-boosted trees, and there is demand for open-weight models that are both accurate and fast at inference across classification and regression.

The technical report introduces three models: Seldon-Mini (27M parameters) and Seldon (213M), both open-weight and handling classification and regression, and the classifier Seldon+. They use an architecture similar to Kumo-Tabular, TabFM and TabPFN-3.5 and are trained on synthetic tables only. Evaluation uses the authors' TabBench (124 classification datasets, plus a missing-values variant) and the authors' own runs of public benchmarks.

Seldon+ ranks first of 15 on TabBench and its missing-values variant, and first on BeyondArena IID classification and TabBench-Bio, second on TabArena classification. On TabArena, Seldon ranks fourth and Seldon-Mini seventh among 109 entries, and both are Pareto-optimal on Elo versus inference time; Seldon is second of 42 on the BeyondArena IID track. Takeaway: a new open-weight synthetic-prior TFM baseline worth adding to TabPFN/TabICL comparisons, especially Seldon-Mini for low-latency use. Caveat: a company technical report; the top rankings come from the authors' own benchmark and their own runs, and Seldon+ weights are not listed as open.

papers.title: InducedTFMs: A Family of Sub-Quadratic Tabular Foundation Models Using Induced Attention
papers.tldr: InducedTFM replaces both attention stages of a bidimensional tabular foundation model with Set Transformer induced attention, making cost linear in rows and features while keeping cell-level representations. At a matched training budget it matches a full-attention TabICLv2 reimplementation on TabArena and reaches a 30x inference speed-up at 640K rows on narrow tables.
summary: Tabular foundation models use attention that is quadratic in the number of samples and features, which limits pretraining to small synthetic tables and forces chunking or subsampling on large tables. Row-compression models cut the feature cost but lose cell-level representations and stay quadratic in samples.

The authors swap both attention stages of a bidimensional TFM for the induced attention of the Set Transformer, which routes attention through a small set of inducing points. This keeps cell-level representations and makes cost linear in both samples and features. They compare against a full-attention TabICLv2 reimplementation under a matched training budget and against a kernel linear-attention baseline of the same asymptotic cost.

InducedTFM matches the full-attention model's accuracy on TabArena and on a benchmark of larger datasets, clearly beats the kernel linear-attention baseline, and becomes faster than TabICLv2 on narrow tables, with a 30x speed-up at 640K rows. Row compression is still preferable on wide tables. Takeaway: induced attention is a drop-in way to scale TFM context to hundreds of thousands of rows without losing cell-level features. Caveat: the comparison is against the authors' reimplementation of TabICLv2, not the released model.

papers.title: Tabular Foundation Models Are Surprisingly Effective In-Context Robot Learners
papers.tldr: TabAct feeds frozen visual features and proprioception as inputs and future action chunks as targets to a frozen tabular foundation model, using each demonstration step as an in-context example. With one demonstration, TabAct with TabICLv2 beats the strongest baseline by 20.9 points on LIBERO and 5.8 on Meta-World, with no robot-specific training.
summary: It is unclear whether models pretrained for generic numerical prediction can act as in-context learners for robot control. Most imitation methods need robot-specific training or target-task fine-tuning.

TabAct casts visual imitation as tabular regression: frozen visual features plus robot proprioception are the inputs, future action chunks are the targets, and every time step of a demonstration is one labeled context example for a frozen TFM that runs closed-loop control. The TFM gets no robot-specific training or fine-tuning; experiments use LIBERO and Meta-World.

With one target-task demonstration per method, TabAct with TabICLv2 has the highest average success on both LIBERO and Meta-World, beating the strongest baseline by 20.9 and 5.8 percentage points. With five demonstrations, success reaches 94.2% on LIBERO-Object without any weight updates. Takeaway: TFMs pretrained on synthetic tables transfer to frozen-feature sequential prediction, another sign that TFM in-context learning works as a general head on top of frozen encoders. Caveat: simulation benchmarks only; no real-robot results are mentioned in the abstract.

papers.title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
papers.tldr: SAE-Audit turns a frozen sparse autoencoder on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct into a clinical concept vocabulary, fits sparse probes on past trials, and feeds the detected concepts with their outcome associations as evidence to a black-box LLM. Without training this raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6 to 12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks.
summary: Predicting clinical-trial outcomes early is valuable, but LLM forecasts are unreliable and their rationales may not reflect the evidence they used. In the author's experiments, frontier LLMs are only modestly above chance at predicting whether a registered trial completes or terminates early.

A frozen SAE on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials select which concepts associate with the outcome. For a new protocol, the detected concepts are written out as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association, and the audited black-box LLM revises its answer given this evidence at inference time.

SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6 to 12.0 points across five clinical-trial prediction tasks and of GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, beating other agentic inference-time optimization methods. The SAE probe module alone is also accurate and yields natural-language explanations from concept contributions. Takeaway: SAE features plus sparse probes can act as an auditable, transferable evidence channel from an open model to a closed one, a practical downstream use of SAEs beyond feature inspection. Caveat: single-author independent work, evaluated on clinical-trial tasks only; code is released.

papers.title: Reward Basis Decomposition for Interpreting Preference Heterogeneity
papers.tldr: Reward Basis Decomposition splits per-user reward weights into a shared population direction and per-user terms, analyzed with concept alignment and SAE decomposition. It recovers planted user directions on synthetic data, but on PRISM and Community Alignment the per-user terms add no reliable predictive benefit: one shared direction explains most preferences.
summary: Reward models define what aligned policies optimize, so understanding the values they encode matters. Existing interpretability methods examine a single reward head and cannot separate values a population shares from values that differ between individuals.

RBD decomposes per-user reward weights into a population term and a per-user term, giving a shared direction and individual user directions in the reward embedding space. Both are interpreted via concept alignment and sparse autoencoder decomposition. The method is first validated on a synthetic control with planted per-user directions and then applied to two real multi-preference datasets, PRISM and Community Alignment.

RBD recovers the planted per-user directions in the synthetic control. On both real datasets it finds no individual-user structure and no reliable predictive benefit from per-user terms beyond the shared population direction under their setup. Takeaway: a useful negative result, suggesting that pluralistic-preference datasets may not contain recoverable per-user directions, and a template for testing that with planted controls before interpreting SAE features of reward models. Caveat: the null result is tied to their setup and the two datasets; the abstract gives no effect sizes. Code and synthetic data are released.

papers.title: SegPFN: Training-Free In-Context Segmentation with Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Networks
papers.tldr: SegPFN treats in-context segmentation as tabular classification: a frozen tabular PFN classifies target-image patches using labeled reference patches as context over frozen visual features. Without segmentation-specific training it improves mean IoU by 4.7 points over the strongest baseline across 11 datasets.
summary: In-context segmentation specifies the target from a few annotated reference images. Training-free approaches rely on hand-designed inference procedures, while learned in-context inference requires segmentation-specific training that can hurt generalization to new domains.

SegPFN extracts frozen visual features, uses labeled reference patches as the context set for a frozen tabular prior-data fitted network, and classifies each target patch. It is benchmarked against major in-context segmentation methods on 11 datasets covering semantic, part and personalized segmentation, with analyses of hard-negative reference patches and joint conditioning on multiple references.

SegPFN improves overall mIoU by 4.7 points over the strongest baseline and has the best average mIoU in four of five task-shot settings. Hard-negative reference patches help fine-grained discrimination, and joint conditioning uses multiple references well. Takeaway: a frozen tabular PFN over frozen patch features is a simple few-shot segmenter, which may be worth trying for medical images such as ultrasound where labeled data is scarce. Caveat: the 11 datasets are general vision benchmarks; medical performance is not reported in the abstract.
